narrative.text: The cover of the Russian edition of the WHO Casebook on ethical issues in international health research, naming its four editors.
A blank page with no extracted text.
The title page of the Russian research ethics casebook, naming the editors, deputy editor and the University of Geneva general editors.

The cataloguing and copyright page of the Russian edition of the casebook, with ISBN, WHO rights and disclaimer notices. It notes that the translation was produced by Ves Mir publishers with the foreign languages department of the First Moscow State Medical University.
The first page of the table of contents of the Russian casebook, listing front matter, the teaching guide and cases in chapters 1 and 2 up to the twin genetics study.
The table of contents continued, listing the remaining chapter 2 cases, chapter 3 on harm and benefit and chapter 4 cases up to post-operative radiotherapy research.
The table of contents continued, listing further consent cases, chapter 5 on standard of care and the start of chapter 6 on obligations to participants and communities.
The table of contents continued, listing chapter 6 cases from mass violence survivors to immunomodulatory HIV therapy and chapter 7 privacy cases up to a vasectomy and prostate cancer study.
The table of contents continued, listing the last privacy cases, chapter 8 on professional ethics, the glossary, recommended readings and appendix.

Acknowledgements for the Russian casebook, crediting the WHO and University of Geneva research ethics training project and its funder. It thanks the many contributors of cases, online discussion organizers, reviewers and design and editorial staff. It is signed by the four editors in March 2009.

The foreword by WHO's Assistant Director-General for information, evidence and research, stressing that sound ethical standards are central to health research and that local researchers and ethics committees need capacity to address ethical issues. It explains that the book uses real cases for individual or group study.

Gives biographies of the casebook's four editors, describing their work in global health research ethics. They include a Harvard specialist who ran early oral rehydration therapy trials, a Harvard professor of population health ethics, the head of WHO's research ethics review committee and a law professor with senior bioethics roles.
A section title page for the introduction, with a WHO photo credit.

Introduces the casebook of 64 cases on difficult ethical questions in planning, reviewing and conducting health research, aimed at researchers and research ethics committees in international studies. It describes use in courses and workshops and notes that cases are real but anonymized. It begins describing WHO's long role in research with Member States and partners.

Explains that the Harvard School of Public Health workshops found case-based discussion guards against cultural bias better than lectures, and that the cases draw on a decade of Harvard and WHO seminars. It also describes WHO's ethics review committee secretariat and its use of cases in training.
A blank page with no extracted text.
A section title page for the teaching guide, with a photo credit.

Introduces the teaching guide for the casebook, explaining that case-based teaching relies on leading structured discussion rather than lecturing. It outlines how the guide covers both process and the content of each chapter, and explains the choice of the term facilitator.

Describes the facilitator's role in shifting focus from lecturer to learners and acknowledges that some teachers may feel uneasy not giving answers. It stresses that the cases have no easy answers and warns against steering learners to a favoured view. It uses the example of treating TB found while screening for an HIV vaccine trial, citing CIOMS and the Declaration of Helsinki.

Lists further discussion questions on researchers' responsibility for conditions outside the study, then advises on selecting cases for a course. It compares beginning a session with the case or with a lecture.

Discusses the advantages of starting with a case or a lecture and recommends splitting large groups into subgroups of six to eight. It advises anticipating responses and challenging both views the facilitator disagrees with and those it shares.

Gives practical tips for leading group discussion, such as encouraging comments, involving everyone, helping second-language speakers and avoiding personal attacks. It also advises periodically summarizing so that open-ended cases still yield key insights.

Begins the chapter-by-chapter guide, noting that cases can be regrouped by theme. It poses questions for chapter 1 on why research must be distinguished from medical care and public health activities. It also asks how physician-researchers should tell patients that interventions aim to generate knowledge.

Continues the chapter 1 questions on the purpose of informed consent, when enrolling patients is inappropriate, vulnerability and whether consent from those with no other access to care is voluntary. It also asks what authorizations might replace ethics review and consent for government-run research.

Suggests using chapter 1 to study the Declaration of Helsinki and CIOMS guidelines and to train ethics committee members. It then introduces chapter 2 on study design, noting ethical problems even in sound designs such as deceptive social psychology experiments.

Recommends Patricia Marshall's monograph on study design and consent in low-resource settings and an Oxford casebook as background. It poses questions on deceptive designs such as the Tearoom Trade study and mystery-client research in Malawi.

Raises justice concerns when groups are excluded from research by age, sex or illness, and whether studies must match national health priorities. It then introduces chapter 3 on harm and benefit, asking what risks are acceptable and who should decide.

Notes growing attention to harms and benefits as more research moves to developing countries, citing microbicide trials and a US bioethics commission report. It discusses the trend toward benefits for families, communities and countries. Questions follow on what is owed to participants and wider communities.

Poses questions on balancing benefits and risks and on whether potential benefits or payments are undue inducements. It then introduces chapter 4 on informed consent, questioning whether standardized consent forms should be exported and whether the term itself is ambiguous.

Discusses how culture and custom may favour decisions by community leaders or male household heads over individual autonomy, and asks how international consent principles apply locally. It also raises questions on literacy, the format of information and who may sign on their own behalf.

Part of the facilitator's guide in the Russian edition of the WHO casebook on ethical issues in international health research, explaining Chapter V on the standard of care and the debate over whether a single universal standard should apply to all trial participants. It recommends the Nuffield Council on Bioethics report on research in developing countries as background. It then lists questions raised by the chapter's cases, such as what international guidelines say about placebo use when effective treatment exists and how the highest attainable standard should be defined.

Continues the facilitator's questions on standards of care, asking whether giving control groups only the local standard exploits vulnerable populations and whether testing a cheaper, less effective intervention can be justified when the best treatment will long remain unavailable locally. It also asks when an ethics committee in a developing country could approve research unacceptable in developed countries, and cites UNAIDS guidance on HIV prevention trials.

Continues the facilitator's guide with Chapter VI on obligations to participants and communities, citing the UNAIDS/AVAC Good Participatory Practice guidelines. It advises facilitators to break the broad topic into specific questions, separating views of what is owed from how obligations are negotiated, and recommends an article on researchers' ancillary care responsibilities. A non-exhaustive list of discussion questions on who bears which obligations follows.

The facilitator's guide to Chapter VII on privacy and confidentiality, suggesting facilitators start by noting that the value placed on privacy varies across cultures and communities. It points to an article on public health and data protection and notes that genomic and data bank issues are not covered by the cases. A list of issues facilitators may raise begins.

Lists privacy questions on extra safeguards for stigmatized conditions such as TB and HIV, anonymization, data access and destruction, and electronic security. It then introduces the facilitator's guide to Chapter VIII on professional ethics, covering conflicts of interest arising from industry funding and practices such as ghostwriting. It ends by asking whether standards of scientific misconduct differ between countries.

Ends the facilitator's guide with questions on which forms of scientific misconduct are most serious and who is responsible for detecting and acting on it, followed by references on case-based learning and assessment.
A section divider page titled case studies.
A blank page with no extractable text.
A divider page for Chapter I, on what research is, with a WHO photo credit.

Opens the Chapter I introduction, explaining that defining research matters because it determines which activities need review by a research ethics committee, and that the definition raises questions of principle. It notes that activities such as surveillance and programme evaluation often involve scientific questions, blurring the line between research and non-research. The page sets out how the chapter's cases explore these boundaries.

Argues that the pursuit of knowledge does not override researchers' duty to protect participants from avoidable harm, recalling Nazi experiments and other abuses before and after the Nuremberg trial. It explains the conflict of goals that arises when doctors act as researchers with their own patients and describes the therapeutic misconception. The page cites the Nuremberg Code.

Explains that sponsors and regulators now require independent research ethics committees to oversee the balance of risks and benefits, because research involves a conflict between scientific and therapeutic goals. It notes that committees cannot oversee risky clinical innovation that is not research, and discusses whether redefining such innovation as research would help. The page cites Beecher's 1966 article on ethics and clinical research.

Notes that research ethics committees probably lack authority over non-research activities such as public health surveillance and some evaluations, even where goals conflict. It discusses examples of surveillance aimed at protecting the public. A recommended reading list follows, including an article on distinguishing audit from research.

Case 1 describes how, during the 2003 SARS outbreak, a national public health centre in country X traced airline passengers who had flown with suspected SARS cases and asked doctors to collect blood samples and medical histories from healthy passengers. Because of delays, testing came after the incubation period, so it could only show possible past contact, yet the centre wanted the data given how little was known about SARS. Questions ask whether this was surveillance, prevention or research and whether ethics approval and specific consent were needed.

Case 2 describes an institute funded by a bilateral agency to run family planning, STI and HIV prevention programmes in developing countries, including adolescent HIV testing and a 100% condom use programme with sanctions on brothels. Its leaders argue that evaluating these low-risk operations needs no ethics review, and the questions ask whether these projects are research and need ethical oversight.

Case 3 describes a neurosurgeon in a large Asian city who has injected olfactory stem cells from aborted fetuses into the brains or spinal cords of over 500 patients with ALS, Parkinson disease, stroke and paralysis. He reports improvements based on videos, functional assessments and e-mailed patient reports, with only pain noted as a side-effect, and foreign patients travel to him. Supporters urged him to run a double-blind trial. Questions ask whether this is research, how efficacy should be judged and who should monitor doctors.

Case 4 describes a university team asked to document quickly the health of an isolated indigenous community in South America after renewed contact with farmers and forestry workers, under tight funding deadlines. It ends with questions on potential harms and benefits and the researchers' duties to any child who falls ill during the study.
A blank page with no extractable text.
A divider page for Chapter II, on issues in study design, with a WHO photo credit.

Opens the Chapter II introduction on scientifically and ethically sound study design, asking whether a protocol's scientific quality is an ethical issue and whether ethics committees should assess it. It separates three tasks: judging the science, judging whether the methods are ethical or a less harmful design would do, and deciding whether better science justifies extra burdens or risks to participants.

States that the second and third tasks are central to ethics committees, while whether they should judge pure science is a practical matter that bodies with peer review expertise could handle. It then explains that controlled trials are needed because many interventions strongly backed by doctors and companies proved ineffective or harmful when properly tested.

Discusses placebo controls, noting the Declaration of Helsinki's caution and listing why different groups prefer placebos, such as doubts about head-to-head trials and sponsors' interests. It explains clinical equipoise as genuine expert uncertainty about which arm is better, and asks how to judge cases where one group seems luckier than another.

Describes misleading trial designs that drug companies may use to favour their products, such as poor blinding, inappropriate analysis or comparator drugs given at ineffective doses, and asks how ethics committees should respond. It then introduces issues of fairness, access and relevance in study design.

Argues that trial participants should come from populations able to benefit from the results, which is a particular concern when sponsors from developed countries test drugs in developing countries where the products may not later be available. It explains that the real benefit of trial participation comes once an intervention is proven safe and useful. It notes that international collaborative research guidelines require research to respond to host country needs.

Describes the role of ethics committees in assessing study design, starting with full understanding of what the protocol aims to learn and how the design affects participants compared with alternatives. It explains that committees may seek design changes if risks are not offset by benefits. A recommended reading list follows, including a WHO/TDR review of ethical challenges in study design in resource-poor settings.

Continues the Chapter II reading list, summarizing articles on using mystery clients without consent to study condom negotiation in Malawi, on including desperate volunteers in trials, and on the meaning of uncertainty and equipoise.

Case 5 notes that nearly 10 million children under five die each year, mostly in developing countries, and describes WHO and UNICEF's Integrated Management of Childhood Illness strategy. It presents a study of how many seriously ill children are referred from primary care to hospital under these guidelines and what happens to them. Questions ask whether the researchers' presence obliges them to help families or health workers with referrals.

A Russian-language case from the WHO casebook on ethics in international health research (case 6), in which an anthropologist plans a study in West Africa where researchers pose as clients to learn how women in sex work negotiate condom use. It raises questions about deceiving participants, confidentiality and whether results should be shared with them. The case is adapted from a published fieldwork account from Ghana.

A Russian-language case (case 7) about a researcher in South Asia who plans to send young men posing as villagers to drug sellers to see what they recommend for a child with diarrhoea. It asks whether such deception is acceptable and whether the sellers should be told about the study afterwards.

A Russian-language case (case 8) on testing a new hepatitis B vaccine for children, giving background on HBV burden and on plasma-derived and recombinant vaccines. It raises ethical questions about trial design and whether consent from one parent is enough for a child's participation.

A Russian-language case (case 9) on preventing TB in people living with HIV, explaining TB's link to HIV and the drugs used for prevention. It describes a trial design of over a decade earlier and the ethical issues it raises for current trials, and credits the case authors at Johns Hopkins.

A Russian-language case (case 10) on developing a malaria vaccine, describing the global malaria burden in 2006 and its causes. It sets out a planned double-blind trial in which children in villages would receive vaccine or placebo after parental consent.

Continues the Russian-language malaria vaccine case, explaining that the team would leave after vaccination and use deaths as the study endpoint because no immune marker exists. It raises questions about allowing natural malaria outcomes in study villages and credits the case authors.

A Russian-language case (case 11) asking whether race should be treated as a risk factor, based on a southern African clinic finding twice as many STI cases among people identifying as "coloured" as among "black" people. It describes the country's history of racial classification and the ethical questions of studying the difference.

A Russian-language case (case 12) on trials of a short course of zidovudine to prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission in the 1990s. It explains why the long "076" regimen was seen as impractical in sub-Saharan Africa and summarises the debate over placebo-controlled trials, citing the Declaration of Helsinki.

Continues the Russian-language zidovudine case with critics' arguments about double standards and placebo controls, followed by discussion questions on whether control groups should receive the long-course regimen and whether such trials are acceptable if they could not run in high-income countries.

A Russian-language case (case 13) on testing the Ayurvedic preparation Ayush-64 for malaria in South Asia, a combination that had never undergone preclinical toxicity testing. It gives background on chloroquine resistance and earlier claims of Ayush-64's effectiveness, and describes the planned study.

Continues the Russian-language Ayush-64 case, describing the randomised comparison with chloroquine and primaquine, how non-responders were switched, and the 28-day follow-up, noting relapse risk if primaquine is not given.

A Russian-language case (case 14) on evaluating a traditional South Asian remedy containing Centella asiatica for bloody diarrhoea, which a researcher wants to test against norfloxacin. It raises questions about trial design given limited antibiotic access in rural areas.

A Russian-language case (case 15) on a population-based twin study in South-East Asia examining genetic and environmental causes of common mental disorders such as alcohol dependence and suicidal thinking. It describes the sample of about 2000 twin pairs and the interviews planned, and raises ethical questions about the study.

A Russian-language case (case 16) on an observational study of newborn care in an East Asian community with high neonatal mortality, where recorders must not intervene. It asks when an observer should step in if she sees harmful practices and what researchers owe participants in observational studies.

A Russian-language case (case 17) in which a recorder in the newborn care study is asked to help treat a family's older child with a high fever. It asks whether she has a personal duty to help and how to handle requests that could compromise her observations.
A Russian-language divider page for Chapter III of the casebook, on harms and benefits.

The Russian-language introduction to Chapter III on harms and benefits, explaining why research can conflict with participants' interests even in ideal conditions. It discusses fairness in choosing participants when benefits outweigh risks and the harms that early-phase trials may cause.

Continues the Russian-language introduction on harms and benefits, stating that ethics committees must ensure risks are minimised and outweighed by benefits and that participants are fully informed. It discusses how hard it is to compare different kinds of harms and benefits, and harms to non-participants, as in xenotransplantation.

Continues the Russian-language chapter introduction with harms to groups, such as stigma from publishing HIV prevalence by village, followed by annotated recommended reading on exclusion of older people from research.
Further Russian-language annotated recommended reading for the harms and benefits chapter, including articles on community engagement in exporting tissue samples and on "scientific imperialism".

A Russian-language case (case 18) on a rotavirus vaccine, describing the disease burden in low-income countries and a ministry's decision to vaccinate all infants despite a risk of intussusception. It notes the plan for a local state company to obtain rights to produce an affordable vaccine.

Continues the Russian-language rotavirus case, in which the North American developer refuses to transfer production technology, citing development costs and liability, and notes the option of compulsory licensing. It asks whether a vaccine causing some intussusception should be used where rotavirus kills many children.

A Russian-language case (case 19) on a pneumococcal vaccine trial in Africa in which 20 000 infants were randomised and vaccinated children stayed free of disease. It raises the question of whether control group children should be vaccinated after the trial.

A Russian-language case (case 20) on early stopping of a randomised trial of a drug to prevent breast cancer recurrence after a data and safety monitoring board recommendation. Its questions ask when researchers may set aside statistical significance for a moral choice.

A Russian-language case (case 21) on pregnancies occurring during a health research study across several countries where legal abortion access varies, many women likely seeking unsafe abortions. It asks what researchers and sponsors should do, including whether to pay for safe abortions and how to warn participants of the risks.

A Russian-language case (case 22) on acting amid conflicting evidence, about non-surgical sterilisation of women with intrauterine quinacrine, used in over 20 countries. It describes reports of cancer that raised concern and the debate over continuing the programmes.

Russian-language discussion questions for the quinacrine sterilisation case, asking whether its use can be justified where maternal mortality is high, whether export of unregistered drugs should be allowed, and what role the scientific community has in policing colleagues.
A Russian-language divider page for Chapter IV of the ethics casebook, on voluntary informed consent.

The Russian-language introduction to Chapter IV on informed consent, tracing its roots to the Nuremberg doctors' trial and the Nuremberg Code, which underpinned the Declaration of Helsinki and CIOMS guidelines. It asks whether consent to research is voluntary, informed and legally valid, and lists source references.

Continues the Russian-language chapter introduction on capacity to consent, covering both legal competence and the ability to understand unfamiliar research concepts. It also discusses how poverty and the offer of care can make consent less than fully voluntary and how ethics committees may respond.

Discusses in Russian what information researchers should give potential participants, listing items such as risks and benefits, study purpose and sponsors, and the difficulty of ensuring real understanding, with references on assessing understanding in HIV vaccine trials.

Explains in Russian the functions of informed consent, such as self-protection and shared responsibility, and exceptions such as emergency research approved through community consultation. It begins to discuss studies whose design requires deception.

Discusses in Russian two types of research involving deception and why it is used in health social science but never in drug trials. It then raises questions about delegating consent to proxies or community leaders.

Continues the Russian-language discussion of community and traditional leaders' roles in consent, noting that the Declaration of Helsinki and CIOMS require individual consent. It also considers subjects who cannot refuse and urges ethics committees to define the purposes of consent for each project.
Russian-language annotated recommended reading on informed consent, including articles on HIV vaccine trials and on the "therapeutic misconception".
Further Russian-language annotated readings on informed consent, including a study of community views on consent in developing countries and an article on openness in genetic research.

A Russian-language case (case 23) on a double-blind trial of high-dose vitamin A for diarrhoea and respiratory infections in children in a traditional West African community. Its questions ask whether individual informed consent is needed there and whom consent is meant to protect.

A Russian-language case (case 24) on a North American university's proposed placebo-controlled trial of tamoxifen as adjuvant therapy for premenopausal breast cancer in South Asia. It describes the standard of care in the US and the researchers' arguments, with footnotes on adjuvant therapy and ovariectomy.

Russian-language questions for the tamoxifen case on whether different consent approaches are justified in a South Asian country and whether research may be done in poor countries because it would not be allowed in rich ones; it also reports outside opinions that not telling women about randomisation was acceptable.

A Russian-language case (case 25) on a vaginal microbicide trial to prevent HIV and other STIs among women. It explains what an ideal microbicide would be and sets out the trial's background and design.

Continues the Russian-language microbicide case, describing monthly check-ups, counselling, condoms and three-monthly HIV tests for participants. It asks, among other things, whether it was ethical not to give HIV test results when antiretroviral therapy was unavailable.

A Russian-language case (case 26) on an 11-year East Asian trial of radiotherapy after surgery for oesophageal cancer, run without ethics committee review, and a journal's critical editorial. Its questions concern publishing unethical research and giving authors a chance to reply.

A Russian-language case (case 27) on a trial of vitamin A and micronutrient supplements for pregnant women in a poor South Asian setting, explaining the link between deficiency, preterm birth and infant death.
Russian-language questions for the micronutrient case on the ethics of randomising communities, the consent process and whether participants must understand randomisation.

A Russian-language case (case 28) on a 1990s Central African study of HIV transmission through breastfeeding by mothers with HIV, which could change the national advice that all mothers breastfeed. It describes the study design and cites WHO's 2006 consensus statement on HIV and infant feeding.
Russian-language questions for the breastfeeding case, on seeking consent from both partners, the husband's role, whether free clinic care is an undue inducement and whether the study was justified.

A Russian-language case (case 29) in which blood donated for dengue vaccine research was used in "humanised mice", and a participant later demanded her anonymised samples be withdrawn. Its questions ask whether she was properly informed.

A Russian-language case (case 30) on obtaining consent from fertility clinic patients to donate surplus embryos for stem cell research, raising questions about consent for research with undefined future aims.

A Russian-language case (case 31) on research into the health needs of older people in a formerly nomadic community in the northern Sahara, in partnership with a European university. It asks whether ethics committees should have reviewed the survey questions.
A Russian-language divider page for Chapter V of the casebook, on the standard of care.

The Russian-language introduction to Chapter V on the standard of care that should be given to control groups in randomised controlled trials in developing countries. It outlines the range of views from a single global standard to context-based standards and cites the Declaration of Helsinki.

Explains in Russian the "single global standard" position, which rejects double standards and is said to match the Declaration of Helsinki, and begins to present the opposing view that cheap local alternatives may matter more to poor populations.

Part of the standard-of-care chapter in the Russian edition of a WHO casebook on ethical issues in international health research, discussing how a sustainable local standard of care might be defined and why sustainability is partly a political choice. It examines the least demanding interpretation, care no worse than what most local participants could normally get, and asks what researchers owe to people found to have unrelated illnesses during screening.

Continues the discussion of standard of care, noting arguments that beneficence and justice make researchers partly responsible for participants' wider well-being, including people excluded from studies. It then lists annotated readings on standards of care and the Declaration of Helsinki debate.

Case 32 describes a 1990s plan by a European company to run a phase III trial of an HIV vaccine among people who inject drugs in a South-East Asian country. The dispute concerns whether participants who seroconvert should receive the best available antiretroviral treatment or only the local standard of care, which critics argued would not be approved in a developed country.

Completes Case 32 with the arguments that top-level treatment would be unsustainable and an undue inducement, then poses discussion questions on the trial's ethics, possible compromises and the company's gifts of equipment to the vaccine institute.

Case 33 concerns a short-course antiretroviral regimen for preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission, tested in southern Africa and then approved by WHO. A later audit found breaches of Good Clinical Practice that raised questions for an East African country seeking to license the drug; notes explain GCP and ICH guidance.

Case 34 introduces quinacrine for non-surgical female sterilization, explaining the unmet need for contraception in developing countries and the method's promotion as cheap and simple despite never being officially approved. Footnotes define surgical tubal sterilization.

Continues Case 34, describing public concern and women's rights groups' objections over quinacrine sterilization trials, given evidence of mutagenicity and doubts about informed consent. It notes how production ceased worldwide and poses questions on population needs, local risk–benefit analysis and double standards.

Case 35 describes a planned randomized trial of a vaginal microbicide to prevent HIV in women, run in East African family planning clinics where patients pay for medicines and Pap smears are unavailable. Trial participants would receive regular STI care, annual Pap smears and free treatment, raising questions about benefits not offered to other clinic users.
A blank page with no extracted text.
The divider page for Chapter VI of the Russian ethics casebook, on obligations to research participants and communities.

Introduces Chapter VI, which treats health research as a partnership whose stakeholders' expectations and obligations should be clear from the start, especially where health care is scarce. It notes that people may join trials to obtain care and that communities may expect researchers to provide it, and asks how far researchers' and sponsors' duties extend.

Lists further areas of obligation, such as continuing effective treatment after a trial ends and caring for unrelated conditions found during research, with an example of paediatricians in an African study area. It notes differing views on whether such duties should be negotiated in advance, guided by respect for persons and justice.

Discusses the narrow view that researchers owe injured participants only emergency care if they disclosed risks, and how negligence can still lead to compensation claims. It then introduces proposals that research should bring benefits to host communities beyond the study itself.

Discusses negotiating fair benefits with host governments and communities, such as training, equipped laboratories or access to proven drugs at cost, proportional to the research burden. It then begins an annotated reading list, including an article on ownership and intellectual property in human tissue samples.
Continues the annotated reading list for Chapter VI, including articles on researchers' ancillary care obligations and on condom provision and counselling in microbicide trials.
Continues the annotated readings, including articles on HIV prevention research and global inequality and on post-trial access to effective interventions for those who still need them.

Case 36 introduces an observational study of cervical cancer, based on a 1970s study, citing global deaths and the role of Pap smears in prevention. It explains the grades of cervical dysplasia, from low-grade lesions that often regress to high-grade precancerous changes.

Continues Case 36, in which women with dysplasia were monitored until carcinoma in situ and then referred with long waits, even after published research showed all dysplasia should be treated. Questions ask about interim reviews, stopping rules, a monitor and whether the results should be published.

Case 37 describes a placebo-controlled trial of a new malaria vaccine for children under five in an East African country, planned jointly by a drug company and local researchers. Background notes explain malaria parasites and the burden of falciparum malaria.

Continues Case 37, where health ministry officials object that the consent process is inadequate given low female literacy and demand free vaccine for all children if it works. Questions address consent, treatment for children who develop malaria and the company's obligations to the wider population.

Case 38 describes a study of the mental health of refugees who survived mass violence, set in a developed country with fragmented services for asylum seekers. It notes that refugees' needs are often misunderstood and defines post-traumatic stress disorder.

Completes Case 38, in which high-risk participants would be referred to public services but no care offered within the study. Questions ask whether an ethics committee should approve an interview that might cause distress and whether researchers should assess or improve referral services.

Case 39 describes a longitudinal community study of rotavirus diarrhoea in children in a poor area of a West African city. The study offers participants free medical services and transport money that will stop when it ends, with results to be given to the health minister.

Poses questions for the rotavirus case on how free services and transport payments might influence mothers' participation and the results, and whether researchers must continue services or help ensure the findings inform health planning.

Case 40 provides background for a childhood cholera vaccine trial, explaining cholera's endemicity in South and South-East Asia and the effectiveness and relative cost of oral and intravenous rehydration and antibiotics. The page ends with notes on tetanus prevention in mothers and newborns.

Case 41 describes a health ministry study in a sub-Saharan African country on how armed conflict has weakened the health system, comparing two population groups. Questions ask about sharing results through local officials and the ethics of grouping internally displaced people with local residents.

Presents, in Russian, case 42 of a WHO casebook on ethics in international health research, on defining a community: a research team in an agricultural district of South Asia where tribal people make up 30% of the population but most of the landless poor. The team, which had collected data mainly in the main village, learns from a local contact how poor the tribal hamlets are.

Continues case 42 in Russian, noting that tribal people made up under 10% of focus group participants and that most received state aid, and asks how the community should be defined and what the sponsors owe; the case was adapted from one supplied in 2007 by Neha Madhiwalla of the Centre for Studies in Ethics and Rights, Mumbai.

Presents case 43, in Russian, on the evaluation of an education programme for disabled children in a poor South Asian democracy, after a campaign made primary education a legal right for all children aged 6–14 and set annual funding per disabled child. An evaluator finds the programme's data were systematically distorted and believes he must make this public, even though the programme may still help children.

Poses questions for case 43, in Russian, on whether the evaluator is right to disclose the distorted data despite possible harm, and how risks to health professionals in such evaluations can be reduced; supplied by Neha Madhiwalla in 2007.

Presents case 44, in Russian, on a large North American randomized trial of an immunomodulating add-on drug for HIV, funded by a company whose agreement gave it ownership of the data. When results suggest the drug does not help, the sponsor refuses to allow publication, and the case asks what the investigator can or should do.

Presents case 45, in Russian, on genetic research in an island population of about 90 000 people whose genetic homogeneity and high rates of some diseases attract researchers looking for disease-linked alleles. A company's deal with the government provokes public protests on religious and democratic grounds, and the company abandons the project to seek samples elsewhere.

Poses questions for case 45, in Russian, on whether a people has collective ownership of its genetic heritage, the ethics of governments negotiating such deals and whether a non-profit sponsor would change the moral picture.
The title page, in Russian, of Chapter VII of the casebook, on privacy and confidentiality.

Introduces Chapter VII, in Russian, explaining that privacy and confidentiality are both interests or rights of individuals and duties of professionals, and can be threatened by research. It discusses who controls access to personal information and how much weight to give privacy when research poses no tangible harm.

Defines confidentiality, in Russian, as a duty not to disclose private information shared within a relationship, and contrasts it with privacy. It argues that privacy concerns should not be overstated where researchers learn private details without causing real harm.

Discusses, in Russian, how to balance personal and public interests, noting that in many societies people have limited control over information about themselves. It warns that researchers studying illegal activity, sex work or drug use usually have no legal protection from court orders to disclose data.

Advises, in Russian, that where data may be subject to compelled disclosure researchers should plan for it and warn participants, and continues with protection of privacy in public health research, ending with a further reading on recent legal and guidance changes.

Presents case 46, in Russian, on a West African trial of nevirapine given to HIV-positive women in labour and their newborns, and asks whether confidentiality about a woman's HIV status should ever be broken and whether staff should plan with her for possible disclosure.

Presents case 47, in Russian, on a European-funded university evaluation of care quality in a South Asian family welfare programme, involving interviews with staff and clients at primary health centres and observation of consultations. It asks what the study leader should advise a researcher facing a confidentiality dilemma, noting the case is similar to case 48.

Presents case 48, in Russian, on the same family welfare evaluation after an ethics committee required that health centres and staff be anonymized. When the findings are later challenged, the case asks whether the promise of confidentiality can be broken and under what conditions.

Presents case 49, in Russian, on a study of complications after abortion in an Eastern European country where legal abortion services are hard to reach and illegal abortions far outnumber legal ones. The design includes safeguards such as private interviews, decoy interviews with other household members and freedom to stop at any time.

Continues case 49, in Russian, describing review by a funder's ethics committee after national approval, and asks what further steps could protect respondents from unwanted attention and whether the way women are recruited is free of coercion.

Presents case 50, in Russian, on a Central American mental health institute that funds community mental health centres for people with severe chronic mental illness and now plans a cost–benefit study of long-term services. Presents case 52, in Russian, on a case-control study in an industrialized country of a possible link between vasectomy and prostate adenocarcinoma, with controls drawn from the electoral register and interviewed by phone. Presents case 53, in Russian, on sociologists studying why women with abnormal Pap smears do not return to hospital for results, with the aim of improving care. It describes the hospital's agreement to the study and gives background on cervical screening.

Presents case 54, in Russian, on a survey of health promotion on a large southern African farm employing seasonal workers, many of them young unmarried women. The researchers observe that many underage girls work there and may be at risk, and are unsure how to act on what they found.

Poses questions for case 54, in Russian, on whether researchers should tell farm management about the underage girls and their risk of sexually transmitted infections including HIV, and what the researchers' moral duties are.

The title page, in Russian, of Chapter VIII of the casebook, on professional ethics.

Introduces Chapter VIII, in Russian, noting the expectation that researchers, ethics committees and sponsors act honestly, with published data not fabricated, falsified or plagiarized and conflicts of interest disclosed. It discusses definitions of conflict of interest and the problem of dual loyalty.

Continues the chapter introduction, in Russian, distinguishing conflicts of goals from conflicts of interest involving personal gain, and describing why such conflicts have become a serious issue in health research involving people, with a reference to the CIOMS ethical guidelines.

Discusses, in Russian, responses to conflicts of interest, noting there is no consensus on whether they are a real ethical problem and that disclosure to journals and ethics committees is the most common response. It then turns to research misconduct, citing studies of researchers' misbehaviour.

Discusses, in Russian, the ethical questions raised in responding to misconduct, such as who should investigate allegations, require evidence, demand retractions and protect both accused scientists and whistle-blowers. It ends with measures such as public trial registration and making raw trial data available for independent checking.

A page of recommended reading (in Russian) for the professional ethics chapter of a WHO casebook on ethical issues in international health research, quoting sources on conflicts of interest in drug trials and on research misconduct. Presents case 56, in which a manufacturer of a new hormonal contraceptive funds regional health researchers to compare pill, patch and injection forms among women of different socioeconomic groups. Discussion questions ask about conflicts of interest and the sponsor's responsibilities to participants.

Presents case 57, in which an Asian drug company contracts an overcrowded long-stay psychiatric hospital in Eastern Europe to carry out further trials of a new schizophrenia drug after cardiac arrhythmias appeared in earlier testing. A note gives background on schizophrenia and its treatability.

Presents case 58, in which a North American university proposing a large family planning evaluation in South-East Asia asks the local ethics committee to review its budget separately from the scientific and ethical review. Questions ask whether ethics committees should examine budgets and how research funding affects the host country.

Presents case 59, in which a mining company's human resources department in West Africa asks European university researchers to estimate the economic cost of the AIDS epidemic to its workforce. The researchers' preliminary findings point to high staff turnover linked to HIV prevalence.

Continues case 59, listing findings on rising medical costs and the need for an in-house treatment programme, and describing the company head's alarm and his wish to shape the report's recommendations. Questions ask how the researchers should respond and whether management should see the report before publication.

Presents case 60, in which a community NGO in a South Asian city partners with researchers to study the health and living effects of a forced slum resettlement, with only one NGO worker involved to keep the study independent. Questions ask about using clinic patients as participants and meeting the community's hopes for direct help.
Ends case 60 with questions on the ethics of researchers being identified with the NGO and of combining service work with research, and credits the source of the case.

Presents case 61, in which a young research assistant finds that a respected scientist altered data to fit the laboratory's hypothesis on lipids and cardiovascular disease. It sets out the reasons the scientist later gave for falsifying data, including pressure to win grants and responsibility for his staff.
Ends case 61 with the scientist's statement and questions on whether his reasons were genuine, how the whistleblower should be treated and who is responsible for research integrity.

Presents case 62, in which six genetics master's students suspect their supervisor of falsifying data in grant applications and raise it with her, but she blames a computer error. Questions ask about the students' options and the university's duties to protect those who raise concerns.

Presents case 63, about a renowned nutrition and immunology researcher who conducted an industry-funded infant formula allergy study, with doubts arising about how the participants were recruited. It goes on to describe a later study of his own multivitamins on memory in older people that a journal editor suspected.

Continues case 63, describing how reviewers doubted the multivitamin study, the researcher claimed the data were lost and the journal asked his university to investigate while he published elsewhere. Questions ask about the roles of universities, governments, professional bodies and journals in dealing with fraud.

Presents case 64, in which a productive researcher leaves an institute in Central America for his home country, leaving unfinished studies and unfunded joint proposals behind. Questions ask who owns the research ideas and who may claim authorship of studies he did not complete.

Continues case 64 with further scenarios on whether a colleague may carry out a study designed by the departed researcher without his permission and how his contribution should be credited in publications.
